A 30-minute lunch break in a Zambian employment contract falls **below the statutory minimum** and is therefore **not lawful**, unless the employee has agreed to an arrangement that is overall more favourable to them (which a shorter break would not be).

---

## The Governing Rule: Section 77, Employment Code Act No. 3 of 2019

Section 77 of the Employment Code Act No. 3 of 2019 sets out the mandatory minimum breaks an employer must grant every employee on each working day:

> *"Subject to an agreement between an employer and an employee which is more favourable to the employee than the provisions of this section, an employer shall grant to the employee on each working day:*
> *(a) a meal break of **one hour**; and*
> *(b) one health break of at least **twenty minutes**, or two health breaks of at least **ten minutes** each."*

[Employment Code Act No. 3 of 2019, Section 77] (Page 47), confirmed at parliament.gov.zm.

---

## What This Means in Practice

| Break Type | Statutory Minimum | 30-min Lunch Break |
|---|---|---|
| Meal break | **1 hour** | 30 minutes (falls short) |
| Health break | 20 min (or 2 x 10 min) | Not separately addressed |

A contract that provides only a 30-minute meal break gives the employee **less** than the one-hour entitlement the law guarantees. That clause would be **void and unenforceable** to the extent it contradicts the Act; the statutory one-hour minimum applies instead.

---

## The Only Exception

The opening words of Section 77 allow a different arrangement **only if it is more favourable to the employee**. A shorter lunch break is less favourable, so it cannot be agreed away. The Act does not permit downward variation of this minimum even by mutual consent.

---

## Practical Takeaway

- **Employers** must provide a full one-hour meal break plus the daily health break(s). A contract providing only 30 minutes is non-compliant.
- **Employees** who are given only 30 minutes are entitled to insist on the full hour under Section 77.
- A Labour Inspector may cite the employer for a breach of the Employment Code Act.

Under the **Employment Code Act No. 3 of 2019** (the governing law, which repealed the old Employment Act), **Section 53** sets out the statutory minimum notice periods as follows:

---

## Notice Periods for Termination of Employment

Where the **contract of employment does not itself specify a notice period**, the employer must give:

| Contract Duration | Minimum Notice |
|---|---|
| Not exceeding 1 month | 24 hours |
| More than 1 month, but not exceeding 3 months | 14 days |
| **More than 3 months** | **30 days** |

**Contracts of more than six months:** the 30-day notice period applies, but with an additional formal requirement: **the notice must be given in writing.** [Employment Code Act No. 3 of 2019, Section 53(2)(c)] (Page 35)

---

## Key Points to Note

1. **Contract may provide a longer period.** The statutory minimums apply only where the contract is silent. A contract can lawfully provide for a longer notice period (and many do, particularly for senior employees), but it cannot contractually reduce the statutory minimum.

2. **Pay in lieu of notice.** If the employer does not give the required notice, they must pay the employee the wages that would have been earned during the notice period. [Section 53(4)]

3. **Employee refuses to work during notice.** If an employee refuses to work out their notice, the employer may deduct the equivalent wages from any terminal payments due. [Section 53(5)]

4. **No notice during leave.** An employer cannot give a notice of termination while an employee is on leave, nor can the notice run concurrently with a period of leave. [Section 53(3)]

5. **Gross misconduct is the exception.** An employee is not entitled to any notice (or compensation in lieu) where they are guilty of misconduct of a nature that makes it unreasonable to require the employer to continue the employment relationship (summary dismissal). [Section 53(1)]

6. **Long-term contracts and gratuity.** Where a long-term contract of employment is terminated under Section 53, the employer must also pay the employee gratuity prorated according to the period of employment. [Section 53(6)]

---

**In short:** for a contract of more than six months, the minimum notice is **30 days, given in writing**, unless the contract itself provides for a longer period, or unless the employer elects to pay 30 days' wages in lieu of notice.

**No.** A business visitor permit in Zambia explicitly does **not** entitle the holder to seek or take up paid employment. Here is the full picture from the governing law.

---

## 1. What a Business Permit Actually Allows

Under **Section 24 of the Immigration and Deportation Act No. 18 of 2010**, a business permit may be issued by an immigration officer to a business visitor for a period **not exceeding 30 days**. The permit must specify:

- The **business the holder is to undertake** (not employment);
- The **person or institution** that invited the visitor or is their point of contact in Zambia;
- The **period** of validity; and
- The **sanctions** for non-compliance with the permit's terms and conditions.

[Immigration and Deportation Act No. 18 of 2010, Section 24] (p. 25)

The **Immigration and Deportation (General) Regulations, SI No. 129 of 2011** go further by printing on the face of the business permit form itself:

> **"This permit does not entitle the holder to seek or obtain paid employment in Zambia."**

(Source: SI 129 of 2011, zambiaimmigration.gov.zm)

---

## 2. The General Prohibition on Working Without a Permit

Taking up employment without the correct permit is a **criminal offence**. The Department of Immigration has obtained convictions on this basis under **Section 54** of the Immigration and Deportation Act No. 18 of 2010, and employers who aid illegal employment face penalties as well.

---

## 3. The Correct Pathway: Two Options

If the business visitor wants to work in Zambia, they must first obtain the appropriate permit:

### (a) Temporary Employment Permit (up to 6 months)
Under **Section 28(10)** of the Act, the Director-General of Immigration may issue a **Temporary Employment Permit (TEP)** to a business visitor who intends to remain in Zambia for **more than 30 days**. The TEP cannot exceed **6 months in any 12-month period**.

Requirements (per the official Zambia Immigration website, zambiaimmigration.gov.zm):
- Covering letter from the institution doing business with the applicant
- Duly completed application Form 25
- Certified copy of valid passport
- One recent passport photo
- Prescribed fee

[Immigration and Deportation Act No. 18 of 2010, Section 28(10)] (p. 27-29)

### (b) Full Employment Permit (over 6 months)
For longer-term employment, a full **Employment Permit** under **Section 28(1)-(6)** is required. Notably, this permit is applied for by the **employer** (not the employee), in consultation with the Ministry responsible for labour. The full permit is valid for up to **5 years** from the date of issue.

---

## 4. Important Note on the Law's Currency

The **Immigration Control Act, 2026** has been passed by Parliament and will repeal the Immigration and Deportation Act No. 18 of 2010. However, the 2026 Act commences only on a date the Minister appoints by statutory instrument, and **no commencement order has been recorded yet**. The 2010 Act therefore remains the governing law for now. You should verify this position with the Department of Immigration (zambiaimmigration.gov.zm) or the Government Gazette before relying on it for a live matter.

---

**In summary:** A business visitor permit is strictly for visiting purposes, not employment. Taking up a job on that permit is unlawful, exposes both the individual and the company to criminal liability, and can result in deportation and prohibition. The correct route is to first obtain either a Temporary Employment Permit (for stays over 30 days, up to 6 months) or a full Employment Permit for longer engagements.

The **Juveniles Act (Cap 53) is no longer the governing law.** It was **repealed in 2022** and replaced by the **Children's Code Act No. 12 of 2022**. The new Act is the statute that now governs the sentencing and disposal of child offenders in Zambia. Below is a full account of both: what the old Act said, and what the law says today.

---

## 1. The Juveniles Act (Cap 53) — What It Said (Historical, Now Repealed)

The Juveniles Act was in force from 4 May 1956 until it was repealed by the Children's Code Act, 2022. Its key sentencing provisions were:

### Section 72 — Restriction on Punishment
- **No child** could be sentenced to **imprisonment or detention in a detention camp.**
- **No young person** could be sentenced to **imprisonment** if he could be suitably dealt with in any other manner.
- A court could not send a child to a **reformatory** unless satisfied, having regard to character, previous conduct, and the circumstances of the offence, that it was expedient for his reformation and the prevention of crime.

### Section 73 — Methods of Dealing with Offenders
A court that found a juvenile guilty could deal with the case by:
- (a) Dismissing the charge
- (b) Making a probation order
- (c) Sending the offender to an **approved school**
- (d) Sending the offender to a **reformatory**
- (e) Ordering the offender to be **caned** (this is a notable provision, discussed further below)
- (f) Ordering the offender to pay a fine, damages, or costs
- (g) Ordering the **parent or guardian** to pay a fine, damages, or costs
- (h) Ordering the parent or guardian to give **security for good behaviour**
- (i) For a young person (not a child): sentencing to **imprisonment**

[Juveniles Act (Cap 53), Sections 72 and 73] (Pages 37-38)

### Section 68 — Language
The words "conviction" and "sentence" were abolished in relation to juveniles, replaced by "finding of guilty" and "order."

---

## 2. The Children's Code Act No. 12 of 2022 — The Governing Law Today

The Children's Code Act repealed the Juveniles Act and represents a comprehensive reform of child justice in Zambia. The sentencing (disposal) framework is fundamentally different in several important ways.

### Section 79 — Methods of Dealing with a Child in Conflict with the Law

A juvenile court or Children's Court **may deal with a child in one or more of the following ways:**
- (a) Dismiss the case or **discharge** the child
- (b) Make a **probation order**
- (c) Send the child to a **child approved centre** or **child reformatory centre**
- (d) Commit the child to the care of a **fit person or child care facility**
- (e) In the case of a young person: order the young person to **pay a fine, damages or costs**
- (f) Order the **parent, guardian or person having parental responsibility** to pay a fine, damages or costs
- (g) Order the parent/guardian to **give security for good behaviour**
- (h) Make a **restorative justice order** under the programmes established by section 84
- (i) Deal with the child in **any other manner** the court determines in the administration of justice

[Children's Code Act, 2022, Section 79(1)] (Page 61)

### Hard Limits on Custodial Orders

- **Section 79(3):** A child **below the age of sixteen** shall **not** be given a custodial order by a court.
- **Section 79(4):** A child **aged sixteen to eighteen** shall **not** be given a custodial order if the child can be suitably dealt with in any other manner.
- **Section 79(5):** A juvenile court or Children's Court shall **not pronounce or record an order of death** against a child. The death penalty is absolutely prohibited for children.

[Children's Code Act, 2022, Section 79(3)-(5)] (Page 62)

### Language: "Conviction" and "Sentence" Prohibited
Section 79(6) reinforces that a court **shall not use the words "conviction" and "sentence"** in relation to a child. The words **"finding of guilty"** and **"order"** are to be used instead.

### Time Limit: Six-Month Rule
Section 79(7) requires courts to deal with a child's case **expeditiously.** If a case is not completed within **six months** of the child's first appearance before the court, the court **may discharge the child immediately.**

[Children's Code Act, 2022, Section 79(6)-(7)] (Page 62)

### Section 100 — Child Approved Centre and Reformatory Orders
Where a **finding of guilty** is made and the order would be for **six months or more without the option of a fine**, and where it is in the **best interests of the child**, the court may:
- (a) Order correction of the child at a **child approved centre**, or
- (b) Require the child to undergo a period of **training at a child reformatory centre**, having regard to the child's character, previous conduct, and the circumstances of the offence.

Any such order **ceases to have effect when the child attains the age of nineteen years.**

[Children's Code Act, 2022, Section 100] (Pages 73-74)

### Section 59 — Diversion (A New Mechanism)
The new Act introduced a formal **diversion** option. A child may be diverted from the formal criminal justice system entirely if:
- (a) There is a likelihood of a prima facie case against the child
- (b) The child **acknowledges responsibility** for the offence
- (c) The child **and** the child's parent/guardian **consent** to the diversion option
- (d) Both understand the consequences of failing to comply

[Children's Code Act, 2022, Section 59] (Page 49)

### Section 113 — Expungement of Records
A finding of guilty against a child is expunged after:
- **5 years**, for a non-residential (non-custodial) order, where the child complied and committed no further offence
- **10 years**, for a residential order (approved centre or reformatory), where the child complied and committed no further offence

**Exception:** Records for **murder, rape, defilement, indecent assault, and aggravated robbery** shall **not** be expunged.

[Children's Code Act, 2022, Section 113] (Pages 80-81)

---

## 3. The Most Significant Changes

| Issue | Juveniles Act (Cap 53) — Repealed | Children's Code Act, 2022 — Current Law |
|---|---|---|
| **Caning** | Expressly allowed (s.73(e)) | **Abolished** — not listed as an option |
| **Death penalty** | Not expressly prohibited | **Absolutely prohibited** (s.79(5)) |
| **Custodial age threshold** | No clear age floor for custodial orders | **Under-16: no custodial order at all** (s.79(3)) |
| **Diversion** | No formal mechanism | **Formal diversion** pathway (s.59) |
| **Restorative justice** | Not provided | **Express option** (s.79(1)(h)) |
| **Record expungement** | Not provided | **Automatic after 5 or 10 years** (s.113) |
| **Time limit for trial** | Not specified | **6 months from first appearance** (s.79(7)) |
| **Language** | "Conviction"/"sentence" abolished (s.68) | Same prohibition, continued (s.79(6)) |

---

**In summary:** the Juveniles Act (Cap 53) is repealed and must not be cited as current law. The **Children's Code Act No. 12 of 2022** is the governing statute. It substantially strengthens protections for child offenders, abolishes caning and the death penalty for children, sets a hard ban on custodial orders for children under sixteen, introduces formal diversion and restorative justice, and provides for expungement of records.

## Joinder of Parties in Zambian High Court Proceedings

### 1. The Primary Rule: Order 14 Rule 5(1) of the High Court Rules

The foundational provision is **Order 14 Rule 5(1) of the High Court Rules (HCR), Chapter 27 of the Laws of Zambia**. Multiple Court of Appeal decisions confirm this as the starting point. The rule provides in full:

> *"If it shall appear to the Court or a Judge, at or before the hearing of a suit, that all the persons who may be entitled to, or claim some share or interest in, the subject-matter of the suit, or who may be likely to be affected by the result, have not been made parties, the Court or a Judge may adjourn the hearing of the suit to a future day, to be fixed by the Court or a Judge, and direct that such persons shall be made either Plaintiffs or Defendants in the suit, as the case may be. In such case, the Court shall issue a notice to such persons, which shall be served in the manner provided by the rules for the service of a writ of summons... and, on proof of the due service of such notice, the person so served, whether he shall have appeared or not, shall be bound by all proceedings in the cause."*

[High Court Rules, Cap 27, Order 14 Rule 5(1)] — confirmed verbatim in *Mpande Limestone Limited v Wadi Fanda Poultry Limited and Idriss Motala* (Appeal No. 002 of 2020) and *2024 HP 1199* (High Court, Chocho J, 7 November 2025).

---

### 2. The Supplementary Rule: Order 15 Rule 6 of the English RSC (The "Whitebook")

Zambian superior courts have recognised a **gap** in Order 14 Rule 5 HCR — notably, it does not expressly deal with cases where a party seeks to add a person between whom and an existing party there is a connected question, and it does not expressly empower an application from a party (as opposed to the court acting on its own motion). To fill this gap, courts apply **Order 15 Rule 6(1), (2) and (3) of the Rules of the Supreme Court of England, 1999 Edition ("The Whitebook")**, which is received English law applicable in Zambia.

The Supreme Court first articulated this in **Hotelier Limited v Odys Works Limited & Finsbury Investments Limited (2012) Vol 2 220 ZR**, and the Court of Appeal has consistently applied it since.

Order 15 Rule 6(2)(b) RSC allows the court, at any stage of proceedings and either on its own motion or on application, to:

> *"order any of the following persons to be added as a party, namely —*
> *(i) any person who ought to have been joined as a party or whose presence before the Court is necessary to ensure that all matters in dispute in the cause or matter may be effectually and completely determined and adjudicated upon, or*
> *(ii) any person between whom and any party to the cause or matter there may exist a question or issue arising out of or relating to or connected with any relief or remedy claimed in the cause or matter which in the opinion of the Court it would be just and convenient to determine as between him and that party as well as between the parties to the cause or matter."*

Order 15 Rule 6(3) RSC adds that an **application by any person** to be added must, except with leave of the Court, be **supported by an affidavit** showing their interest in the matters in dispute.

[Confirmed verbatim in *Mpande Limestone Limited v Wadi Fanda Poultry Limited and Idriss Motala*, Appeal No. 002 of 2020, pp. J16-J17, Court of Appeal]

---

### 3. The Three-Part Test for Joinder

The Court of Appeal in **Mpande Limestone Limited v Wadi Fanda Poultry Limited and Idriss Motala (Appeal No. 002 of 2020)** distilled the combined effect of Order 14 Rule 5(1) HCR and Order 15 Rule 6 RSC into the following authoritative three-part test. A party satisfies the threshold if they meet **any one** of three requirements:

1. They are persons who **may be entitled to, or claim some share or interest** in the subject-matter of the suit, or who **may be likely to be affected by the result**;
2. They are persons **whose presence before the Court is necessary** to ensure that all matters in dispute may be effectually and completely determined and adjudicated upon; or
3. They are persons **between whom and any existing party there exists a question or issue** arising out of or connected with any relief or remedy claimed in the cause, which in the opinion of the Court it would be just and convenient to determine alongside the existing dispute.

[*Mpande Limestone*, Appeal No. 002 of 2020, at J18; also applied in *2024 HP 1199*, 2024 HP 1557, and *Bell Equipment Zambia Limited v Foveros Mining Limited*, Appeal No. 0126 of 2021]

---

### 4. Key Procedural Points

| Point | Rule / Authority |
|---|---|
| Who may apply | Any party, or the court on its own motion (mero motu) | Order 14 Rule 5(1) HCR; Order 15 Rule 6(2) RSC |
| Supporting document | Affidavit in Support showing interest | Order 15 Rule 6(3) RSC |
| Mode of application | Inter Partes Summons (Notice of Motion in chambers) | Standard HCR practice |
| Timing | "At or before the hearing" — courts have confirmed it may be made at any stage, even after cross-examination | *Mpande Limestone*, Appeal No. 002 of 2020, at J19 |
| Even on appeal | A court of appeal may raise joinder mero motu to safeguard third-party interests | App No. 47 of 2025 (Court of Appeal) |
| Service on the new party | By notice served in the manner prescribed for a writ of summons | Order 14 Rule 5(1) HCR |
| Non-joinder is not fatal | No cause or matter shall be defeated by reason of misjoinder or non-joinder | Order 15 Rule 6(1) RSC |

---

### 5. Leading Cases to Cite

| Case | Court | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| *Hotelier Limited v Odys Works Limited & Finsbury Investments Limited* (2012) Vol 2 220 ZR | Supreme Court | Confirmed gap in Order 14 Rule 5 HCR; directed resort to Order 15 Rule 6 RSC |
| *Mpande Limestone Limited v Wadi Fanda Poultry Limited and Idriss Motala*, Appeal No. 002 of 2020 | Court of Appeal | Binding authority setting out the three-part test |
| *Bell Equipment Zambia Limited v Foveros Mining Limited*, Appeal No. 0126 of 2021 | Court of Appeal | Applied the three-part test to a surety/director joinder |
| *Mike Hamusonde Mweemba v Kamfwa Obote Kasongo & Zambia State Insurance Corporation Limited (Intended Joinder)* (2006) ZR 101 | Supreme Court | Frequently cited on joinder principles |
| *Attorney General v Tall & Zambia Airways Corporation Limited* (1995-1997) ZR 54 | Supreme Court | Foundational on joinder |
| *Zulu v Avondale Housing Project Limited* (1982) ZR 172 | Supreme Court | Classic authority on parties and joinder |
| *Solomon Laban Jumbe Ngwenya v Hope Chanda*, Appeal No. 1 of 2021 | Court of Appeal | Confirmed same elements apply to misjoinder applications |

---

### Practical Note

A defendant wishing to join another party files an **Inter Partes Summons** supported by an **Affidavit in Support** showing the intended party's interest or the connection of the issue, grounding the application in **Order 14 Rule 5(1) HCR as read together with Order 15 Rule 6(2)(b) and (3) of the RSC (1999 Edition)**. The application can be brought at any stage before judgment. The court does not have a separate Zambian "third-party procedure" equivalent to England's former Order 16 RSC; the joinder route under Order 14/15 is the mechanism used for all cases, including where a defendant seeks to bring in a party from whom it claims contribution or indemnity.

**The Public Gathering Bill, 2026 has NOT yet been enacted into law.** As of now, it remains a Bill before the National Assembly of Zambia (Bill No. 71 of 2026, introduced 23 April 2026). It still appears on the National Assembly's Bills list at parliament.gov.zm and has not moved to the Acts list. The law currently governing public gatherings remains the **Public Order Act, 1955 (Cap. 113)**, which this Bill proposes to repeal and replace.

Here is a detailed breakdown of what the Bill proposes:

---

## The Public Gathering Bill, 2026 (N.A.B. 71 of 2026)

### Purpose and Background

The Bill was introduced by the Attorney-General (M.D. Kabesha) and has four stated objects:

1. Promote protection of the **freedom of assembly and association** at a public gathering.
2. **Regulate the conduct** of public gatherings for the preservation of public order and safety.
3. **Repeal and replace** the Public Order Act, 1955 (Cap. 113).
4. Provide for incidental matters.

[The Public Gathering Bill, 2026, Memorandum]

---

### Key Definition

A **"public gathering"** is defined as *an assembly, meeting, procession or demonstration of three or more people in a public place.* A "public place" includes highways, market places, squares, roads, streets, bridges, and any place to which the public has access (with or without payment). [Clause 2]

---

### Who is Exempt?

The Bill does **not** apply to gatherings held by (Clause 3):

- The President or Vice-President
- The Speaker, First or Second Deputy Speaker
- A Minister or Provincial Minister
- A Member of Parliament performing functions in their constituency
- A Mayor, council chairperson, or councillor performing civic duties in their area
- Public officers performing Government functions
- Religious meetings in registered places of worship
- Funerals, traditional ceremonies, and wedding ceremonies
- Indoor meetings of companies, NGOs, trade unions, or registered organisations
- Indoor meetings of organs of a registered political party discussing party affairs
- Meetings of State institutions

**However**, the exemptions for Speakers, Ministers, MPs, and local government officials do **not** apply during an election campaign, an election, or when Parliament is dissolved. [Clause 3(3)]

---

### Notice Requirement (The Core Procedure)

An organiser must **notify an authorised officer at least 5 days before** the proposed gathering, delivering notice to the police station in the relevant area. The notice must include: [Clause 6]

- Location, date and time
- Route and destination (for processions)
- Purpose of the gathering
- Estimated number of participants
- Name and contact details of the organiser
- Safety and control arrangements
- An undertaking to cooperate with police to ensure peace and order

**Authorised officers** are defined as the Inspector-General of Police, Divisional Commanders, Officers Commanding-District, officers-in-charge of police stations, or any authorised police officer. [Clause 2]

---

### Approval and Restriction Process

| Step | Timeframe | Provision |
|------|-----------|-----------|
| Acknowledgment of notice | Within **24 hours** of receipt | Clause 7 |
| Approval of the gathering | Within **3 days** of receipt | Clause 8 |
| If no acknowledgment within 24 hrs | Notice **deemed received** | Clause 7(2) |
| If no approval after deemed receipt | Organiser **may proceed** | Clause 8(3) |

An authorised officer may attach **conditions** to an approval for public order/safety purposes. [Clause 8(2)]

An officer may **restrict** a gathering where: [Clause 9]
- A prior notice exists for the same date, time, and venue
- The venue is unsuitable for crowd/traffic control, interferes with other lawful business, or is within a protected area
- There is a reasonable belief the gathering is likely to cause public disorder, property damage, or danger to public safety

Where restricted, the organiser must be informed **in writing, at least 3 days before**, with reasons, and must be invited to take remedial measures.

---

### Duties of the Authorised Officer

Officers must (Clause 4):
- Protect and promote freedom of peaceful assembly, expression, movement, freedom from arbitrary arrest, and freedom from torture or degrading treatment
- Act without partiality
- Ensure the right of assembly is balanced against public order and safety
- Intervene only where there is **imminent danger** to public order or safety
- Minimise disruption (traffic, access to property, injury prevention)

They may order **dispersal** only where a gathering poses a **direct and imminent threat** to public order or safety that cannot otherwise be contained, or is likely to result in loss of life. [Clause 4(2)]

---

### Media Rights

Authorised officers, organisers, participants, and any other persons must **respect and uphold the right of the media to monitor** a public gathering. [Clause 10]

---

### Offences and Penalties

| Offence | Penalty |
|---------|---------|
| Wearing attire associated with the Defence Force or security services at a gathering | Fine of 20,000 penalty units **(K8,000)** or up to 2 months' imprisonment, or both [Clause 11(3)] |
| Possessing a firearm or weapon at a public gathering | Fine of up to 500,000 penalty units **(K200,000)** or up to 5 years' imprisonment, or both [Clause 12(2)] |
| Holding an unauthorised gathering (no notice, in contravention of a restriction, or contrary to the Act) | Fine of up to 50,000 penalty units **(K20,000)** or up to 3 months' imprisonment, or both; or community service/probation [Clause 13(2)] |

*Penalty unit value: K0.40 per unit, per Statutory Instrument No. 25 of 2024. Confirm the current value before relying on these figures.*

---

### Appeals

A person aggrieved by a decision of an authorised officer may appeal: [Clause 15]
1. **First**, to the **Minister** within 14 days of the decision
2. **Then**, to the **High Court** within 14 days of the Minister's decision

---

### Immunity

Authorised officers are protected from legal action for acts done **in good faith** in the exercise of their functions under the Act. [Clause 16]

---

## Key Takeaway

The Bill represents a significant shift from the colonial-era Public Order Act, 1955. Rather than requiring **police permission** before a gathering (the current regime), the Bill moves to a **notification system** where an organiser gives notice and may, in some circumstances, proceed even without formal approval. It also explicitly places duties on police to **protect** the right of assembly, not merely to regulate it. That said, the restriction and dispersal powers remain, and the exemptions for senior government officials have attracted public commentary.

**It is not yet law.** Parliament must pass it and the President must assent to it before it takes effect. Confirm the Bill's progress at [parliament.gov.zm](https://www.parliament.gov.zm/publications/bills-list).

## Convicting on Circumstantial Evidence: The Zambian Standard

The governing principles come from **David Zulu v The People**, the Supreme Court of Zambia decision described across multiple Court of Appeal judgments as "the leading and probably most cited authority on circumstantial evidence" in Zambia. It binds all lower courts. The Court of Appeal has consistently restated and applied its principles in APP No. 164 of 2018, APP No. 002 of 2022, APP No. 52 of 2022, APP No. 218 of 2020, and APP No. 404142 of 2020.

---

### What Circumstantial Evidence Is

Circumstantial evidence is **not direct proof** of the fact in issue. It is proof of *other* facts (not themselves in issue) from which an **inference** about the fact in issue may be drawn. This indirect quality is described as a built-in weakness of the category, and the law responds to that weakness with a heightened standard before a conviction is permitted.

[APP No. 164 of 2018, Court of Appeal; APP No. 002 of 2022, Court of Appeal]

---

### The Three Things a Trial Judge Must Do

**1. Guard against wrong inferences**

The trial judge is positively obliged to "guard against drawing wrong inferences from the circumstantial evidence at his disposal before he can feel safe to convict." This is a gatekeeping duty: the judge must actively interrogate the inferences the evidence supports, not simply accept the most obvious one.

[APP No. 52 of 2022; APP No. 169/170/171 of 2020, Court of Appeal]

**2. Satisfy themselves that the evidence reaches the required degree of cogency**

The circumstantial evidence must have "taken the case out of the realm of conjecture so that it attains such a degree of cogency which can permit **only** an inference of guilt." Suspicion, probability, or even likelihood is not enough. The evidence must exclude all reasonable alternative explanations.

[APP No. 002 of 2022; APP No. 164 of 2018, Court of Appeal]

Stated another way: "the inculpatory facts must be incompatible with the innocence of the accused and incapable of explanation upon any other hypothesis than that of the accused's guilt." [APP No. 002 of 2022]

**3. Resolve any competing reasonable inference in favour of the accused**

Where the evidence supports more than one inference, the judge must adopt "an inference more favourable to the accused person." A conviction cannot follow if the evidence is equally consistent with innocence.

[APP No. 169/170/171 of 2020, Court of Appeal]

---

### The Accused's Explanation: A Separate Hurdle

Even where the three conditions above are met, there is a further check: **if the explanation given by the accused may reasonably be true, a conviction cannot ensue.** The prosecution must, in effect, negative a reasonable exculpatory account.

> "It is trite that a conviction can properly be anchored on purely circumstantial evidence. The only requirement is that it must be sufficient enough to permit only an inference of guilt. Further, if the explanation given by an accused person may reasonably be true, a conviction cannot ensue."

[APP No. 218 of 2020, Court of Appeal]

---

### What Happens When a Trial Court Gets It Wrong

In APP No. 218 of 2020, the Court of Appeal quashed a conviction precisely because the trial court had failed to properly evaluate the circumstantial evidence and had drawn an inference of guilt when that was not the *only* inference available on the facts. The court held that "if the trial court properly evaluated the circumstantial evidence herein, it would have found that it is insufficient and could not permit only an inference of guilt."

---

### Summary in One Sentence

Before convicting on circumstantial evidence, a trial judge must be satisfied that the combined weight of the evidence points so exclusively to guilt that no other reasonable inference is open, that the accused's reasonable explanation (if any) has been excluded, and that the conviction is not built on conjecture.

Estoppel is a common law doctrine (received into Zambian law through English common law) that prevents a person from going back on a statement, representation, or position they previously adopted, when doing so would be unjust to someone who relied on it. Zambian courts apply it regularly. Here is how they have explained and categorised it:

---

## The Core Principle

The Court of Appeal in **APP No. 93 of 2020** adopted the classic statement of Lord Denning MR in *Moorgate v Twitchings*:

> *"When a man by his words or conduct has led another to believe in a particular state of affairs, he will not be allowed to go back on it when it would be unjust and inequitable for him to do so."*

In plain terms: if you cause someone to act on the basis of something you said or did, you cannot later contradict it to their detriment.

---

## The Main Types of Estoppel

### 1. Estoppel by Conduct (Representational Estoppel)
This arises where one person **induces another to adopt and act upon an assumption of fact**, or an assumption about the representor's future conduct. The Court of Appeal (APP No. 93 of 2020) held that once such conduct is shown, the representor "is prevented from going back on the words or conduct which led the other person to act on that basis."

**Practical example from that case:** A bank that requested its client to put it in funds when a performance guarantee was called upon was held estopped by its own conduct from later denying that it had issued the guarantee.

---

### 2. Judicial Estoppel
This prevents a party from **taking contradictory positions in the same litigation or successive proceedings**. The Court of Appeal in **APP No. 170 of 2025** described it this way:

> *"Judicial estoppel prevents a party from taking a position in litigation that contradicts a position previously asserted if the court accepted the earlier position. It is meant to preserve the integrity of the judicial process by prohibiting parties from 'criss-crossing' or changing positions to suit their needs at different stages of litigation."*

The court cited the Supreme Court's ruling in *Zambia Revenue Authority v Professional Insurance Corporation Limited* as authority for the principle that a party relying on a statute cannot simultaneously argue that the same statute does not apply to them. [APP No. 170 of 2025, p. 18-19]

---

### 3. Cause of Action Estoppel
This bars a party from **re-litigating a cause of action** that has already been determined in earlier judicial or arbitral proceedings. As summarised by the Court of Appeal in **APP No. 92 of 2020**, citing Lord Sumption JSC in *Virgin Atlantic Airways Ltd v Zodiac Seats UK Ltd*:

> *(1) Cause of action estoppel is absolute in relation to all points which had to be and were decided in order to establish the existence or non-existence of a cause of action.*
> *(2) It also bars the raising of points essential to the cause of action which were not raised in the earlier proceedings, if they could with reasonable diligence and should in all circumstances have been raised.*

---

### 4. Issue Estoppel
Closely related, this **precludes a party from challenging a specific issue** already decided in earlier proceedings, even if the overall cause of action is different. The Court of Appeal (APP No. 92 of 2020) stated:

> *"Except in special circumstances where this would cause injustice, issue estoppel bars the raising in subsequent proceedings of points which (i) were not raised in the earlier proceedings or (ii) were raised but unsuccessfully."*

---

## Key Things to Note

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Legal basis** | Common law doctrine, received into Zambian law via the English Law (Extent of Application) Act, Cap 11 (English law as at 17 August 1911 is binding in Zambia) |
| **It is a defence, not a cause of action** | Estoppel bars a party from asserting something; it does not by itself create a right |
| **Must be pleaded** | The Court of Appeal (APP No. 93 of 2020) confirmed that estoppel must be pleaded and raised in evidence; a court cannot apply it on its own initiative without giving the other side an opportunity to respond |
| **Equity-based** | It is rooted in fairness and prevents unconscionable behaviour |

---
